extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, literary critics, and poets studying poetic/tragedy theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic guidance and evaluative criteria for poetry (especially tragedy) drawn from classical and critical traditions (Plato, Aristotle, Aristophanes, later critics). Useful for judging or composing poetic drama with respect to moral, aesthetic, and structural standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral excellence of the poet
rubrics_metrics.description: “No one can be a good poet who is not first a good man.” (Strabo/Plutarch sentiment that the excellence of a poet is bound up with that of the human being.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical tradition holds the poet’s personal goodness as a criterion of poetic worth — the poet’s moral character affects reception and authority. Cited as a prevailing Greek view influencing later thought (Minturno, Plutarch references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as preparatory/didactic for youth
rubrics_metrics.description: “Poetry is the preparatory school of philosophy.” — it ‘opens and awakens the youthful mind’ by blending truth with fiction so young readers may be prepared to accept philosophical doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aimed at youth, poetry should mix fiction and truth gently (a ‘twilight’ before full philosophical light). Emphasizes painless moral/intellectual initiation rather than direct doctrinal instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as moral and political adviser (comic poet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristophanes’ claim that the comic poet “not only ministers to the enjoyment of the community and educates their taste, he is also a moral teacher and political adviser” and that ‘Comedy too is acquainted with justice.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this view comedy (and by extension poets) should mix earnest moral counsel with entertainment; satire should target the unworthy (not what is honest and true), and the poet may serve civic moral purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic pleasure as the primary end of poetry (Aristotle)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The object of poetry, as of all the fine arts, is to produce an emotional delight, a pure and elevated pleasure.” Instruction is secondary; delight is the chief end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should be judged primarily by its capacity to produce refined aesthetic pleasure; moral instruction is incidental and subordinate to the artistic end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth distinct from scientific or historical truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “The standard of correctness in poetry and politics is not the same... poetical truth and scientific truth are not identical.” Technical inaccuracies in medicine, natural history etc. do not touch the essence of the poetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate poetic works by factual/scientific accuracy; assess them by their own poetic/logical/aesthetic laws (probability, necessity, plausibility within the work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tragedy — imitation of a serious, complete action of magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: “Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude.” (μίμησις πράξεως σπουδαίας, καὶ τελείας μέγεθος ἐχούσης)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragic plot should present a whole, serious action with sufficient scope (magnitude) to be significant; the action must be complete (having beginning, middle, end) and weighty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy: language embellished with several kinds of artistic ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy uses language ‘embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play’ (verse and song; verse in dialogue, lyrical song in choral parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different modes of embellishment belong to different parts (dialogue = verse, chorus = lyric/song). Use appropriate formal ornaments in their proper dramatic locations; avoid mixing ornamentation indiscriminately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy must be in the form of action (dramatic), not narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is in the ‘form of action, not of narrative’ — it must present enacted incidents rather than mere report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic presentation (showing characters acting) is essential; reliance on narrated events undermines the tragic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy’s function: catharsis via pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy works ‘through pity and fear effecting the proper katharsis, or purgation, of these emotions.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful tragedy should arouse pity and fear and bring about their appropriate catharsis (emotional purification/relief) in the audience; this emotional effect is a key test of dramatic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of vice allowed only by necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The representation of moral depravity finds its only excuse in ‘necessity.’ ... Gratuitous or motiveless depravity is... forbidden.” (Aristotle: vice is permissible only when demanded by the plot's inner necessity.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depiction of immoral actions must be motivated by the structural needs of the plot (probability/necessity); avoid gratuitous depravity or sensationalism that has no artistic justification (example: Menelaus in Orestes cited as faulty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should represent the general, not the particular (avoid personal satire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle condemns personal satire as inferior because ‘art ought to represent the general not the particular.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poetic/dramatic art abstracts general types and universal truths rather than targeting individuals or particular scandals; personal invective weakens artistic universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of structure and inevitability of sequence (ethical/aesthetic consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle praises works (e.g., Sophocles) for ‘unity which pervades the structure of his dramas, and the closely linked sequence of parts which work up to an inevitable end.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess structure for unity and tight causal linkage — incidents should follow by necessity or probability towards an inevitable catastrophe/resolution; avoid inartistic structure, bad character-drawing, and misapplied choral parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters: σπουδαῖοι / χρηστά — heroically elevated, not mere ordinary goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle requires characters that are of the heroic/‘noble’ order (σπουδαῖοι) — moral grandeur/‘greatness’ that lifts them above ordinary life; goodness may be poetic/idealized rather than plain virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters in epic/tragedy should be elevated or idealized to produce grandeur; poetic ennoblement is permissible (defective traits can be ennobled) but mere wickedness or trivial virtue is inappropriate for the higher forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sentimentalism and debased pity
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of Euripides: he ‘substitutes the troubling of the senses for genuine tragic emotion’ — tragic pity must not be debased into ignoble sentimentalism (rags, stage-properties of woe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on cheap, sensory contrivances to manufacture emotion; aim for genuine tragic feeling grounded in character and plot necessity rather than melodramatic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic evaluation should consider moral content but prioritize aesthetic laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: moral content and author’s character are important to the total impression, but the test of excellence is pleasure and the work must be judged by its own laws rather than moral/political criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing poetry, note ethical tendencies as contributing to the overall impression, but evaluate according to poetic principles (form, unity, probability, catharsis) first. Moral defects matter only insofar as they disturb the aesthetic ideal (sane, wholesome pleasure).
